claim: SIRT6 is a sirtuin with established tumor suppressor function.
source: SIRT6, a sirtuin with established tumor suppressor function, regulates the lysine fatty acylation of R-Ras2.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about SIRT6.

claim: Sirt6 knockout increased R-Ras2 lysine fatty acylation in mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: In mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs), Sirt6 knockout (KO) increased R-Ras2 lysine fatty acylation.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation promotes the plasma membrane localization of R-Ras2.
source: Lysine fatty acylation promotes the plasma membrane localization of R-Ras2 and its interaction with phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase PI3K, leading to activated Akt and increased cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by confocal imaging data in Figure 2J and subcellular fractionation data.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation promotes R-Ras2 interaction with PI3K.
source: Lysine fatty acylation promotes the plasma membrane localization of R-Ras2 and its interaction with phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase PI3K, leading to activated Akt and increased cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4A.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation of R-Ras2 leads to activated Akt.
source: Lysine fatty acylation promotes the plasma membrane localization of R-Ras2 and its interaction with phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase PI3K, leading to activated Akt and increased cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Western blot data showing p-Akt levels in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation of R-Ras2 leads to increased cell proliferation.
source: Lysine fatty acylation promotes the plasma membrane localization of R-Ras2 and its interaction with phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase PI3K, leading to activated Akt and increased cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by cell proliferation assays in Figure 4D.

claim: SIRT6 belongs to the Sir2 family of NAD+-dependent protein lysine deacylases.
source: SIRT6 (sirtuin 6) belongs to the Sir2 (silencing information regulator 2) family of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+)-dependent protein lysine deacylases.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Introduction.

claim: SIRT6 plays important roles in DNA damage and repair.
source: It plays important roles in a variety of biological processes, including DNA damage and repair (Kaidi et al., 2010; Mao et al., 2011; Toiber et al., 2013), glucose metabolism (Zhong et al., 2010), and cell proliferation (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SIRT6 plays important roles in glucose metabolism.
source: It plays important roles in a variety of biological processes, including DNA damage and repair (Kaidi et al., 2010; Mao et al., 2011; Toiber et al., 2013), glucose metabolism (Zhong et al., 2010), and cell proliferation (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SIRT6 plays important roles in cell proliferation.
source: It plays important roles in a variety of biological processes, including DNA damage and repair (Kaidi et al., 2010; Mao et al., 2011; Toiber et al., 2013), glucose metabolism (Zhong et al., 2010), and cell proliferation (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sirt6 knockout mice display multiple defects and die a few weeks after birth.
source: Sirt6 knockout (KO) mice display multiple defects and die a few weeks after birth (Mostoslavsky et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SIRT6 can deacetylate histone H3 lysine 9.
source: It can deacetylate histone H3 lysine 9 (Ac-H3K9), lysine 18 (Ac-H3K18), and lysine 56 (Ac-H3K56) (Michishita et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2009; Michishita et al., 2009; Tasselli et al., 2016), to suppress target gene expression of several transcription factors, including NF-κB (Kawahara et al., 2009), HIF-1α (Zhong et al., 2010), c-Jun (Sundaresan et al., 2012), and c-Myc (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SIRT6 can deacetylate histone H3 lysine 18.
source: It can deacetylate histone H3 lysine 9 (Ac-H3K9), lysine 18 (Ac-H3K18), and lysine 56 (Ac-H3K56) (Michishita et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2009; Michishita et al., 2009; Tasselli et al., 2016), to suppress target gene expression of several transcription factors, including NF-κB (Kawahara et al., 2009), HIF-1α (Zhong et al., 2010), c-Jun (Sundaresan et al., 2012), and c-Myc (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SIRT6 can deacetylate histone H3 lysine 56.
source: It can deacetylate histone H3 lysine 9 (Ac-H3K9), lysine 18 (Ac-H3K18), and lysine 56 (Ac-H3K56) (Michishita et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2009; Michishita et al., 2009; Tasselli et al., 2016), to suppress target gene expression of several transcription factors, including NF-κB (Kawahara et al., 2009), HIF-1α (Zhong et al., 2010), c-Jun (Sundaresan et al., 2012), and c-Myc (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SIRT6 suppresses target gene expression of NF-κB.
source: It can deacetylate histone H3 lysine 9 (Ac-H3K9), lysine 18 (Ac-H3K18), and lysine 56 (Ac-H3K56) (Michishita et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2009; Michishita et al., 2009; Tasselli et al., 2016), to suppress target gene expression of several transcription factors, including NF-κB (Kawahara et al., 2009), HIF-1α (Zhong et al., 2010), c-Jun (Sundaresan et al., 2012), and c-Myc (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SIRT6 suppresses target gene expression of HIF-1α.
source: It can deacetylate histone H3 lysine 9 (Ac-H3K9), lysine 18 (Ac-H3K18), and lysine 56 (Ac-H3K56) (Michishita et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2009; Michishita et al., 2009; Tasselli et al., 2016), to suppress target gene expression of several transcription factors, including NF-κB (Kawahara et al., 2009), HIF-1α (Zhong et al., 2010), c-Jun (Sundaresan et al., 2012), and c-Myc (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SIRT6 suppresses target gene expression of c-Jun.
source: It can deacetylate histone H3 lysine 9 (Ac-H3K9), lysine 18 (Ac-H3K18), and lysine 56 (Ac-H3K56) (Michishita et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2009; Michishita et al., 2009; Tasselli et al., 2016), to suppress target gene expression of several transcription factors, including NF-κB (Kawahara et al., 2009), HIF-1α (Zhong et al., 2010), c-Jun (Sundaresan et al., 2012), and c-Myc (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SIRT6 suppresses target gene expression of c-Myc.
source: It can deacetylate histone H3 lysine 9 (Ac-H3K9), lysine 18 (Ac-H3K18), and lysine 56 (Ac-H3K56) (Michishita et al., 2008; Yang et al., 2009; Michishita et al., 2009; Tasselli et al., 2016), to suppress target gene expression of several transcription factors, including NF-κB (Kawahara et al., 2009), HIF-1α (Zhong et al., 2010), c-Jun (Sundaresan et al., 2012), and c-Myc (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SIRT6 has been reported to be an ADP-ribosyltransferase.
source: SIRT6 has also been reported to be an adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-ribosyltransferase (Mao et al., 2011; Liszt et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SIRT6 is an efficient lysine defatty-acylase that regulates the secretion of TNFα.
source: We have recently identified SIRT6 as an efficient lysine defatty-acylase that regulates the secretion of tumor necrosis factor (TNFα) (Jiang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation promotes TNFα targeting to lysosome and decreases its secretion.
source: Mechanistically, lysine fatty acylation promotes TNFα targeting to lysosome and thus decreases its secretion (Jiang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The Ras family of proteins plays important roles in signal transduction.
source: The Ras family of proteins plays important roles in numerous biological pathways, including signal transduction, membrane trafficking, nuclear export/import, and cytoskeletal dynamics (Wennerberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The Ras family of proteins plays important roles in membrane trafficking.
source: The Ras family of proteins plays important roles in numerous biological pathways, including signal transduction, membrane trafficking, nuclear export/import, and cytoskeletal dynamics (Wennerberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The Ras family of proteins plays important roles in nuclear export/import.
source: The Ras family of proteins plays important roles in numerous biological pathways, including signal transduction, membrane trafficking, nuclear export/import, and cytoskeletal dynamics (Wennerberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The Ras family of proteins plays important roles in cytoskeletal dynamics.
source: The Ras family of proteins plays important roles in numerous biological pathways, including signal transduction, membrane trafficking, nuclear export/import, and cytoskeletal dynamics (Wennerberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Five branches of the Ras superfamily are classified according to sequence similarity: Ras, Rho, Rab, Arf, and Ran.
source: Five branches of the Ras superfamily (Ras, Rho, Rab, Arf, and Ran) are classified according to sequence similarity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Ras protein classification.

claim: Ras proteins can exist in a GDP-bound inactive state and a GTP-bound active state.
source: Ras proteins can exist in two conformational states: a GDP-bound inactive state and a GTP-bound active state.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Ras protein function.

claim: In the GTP-bound state, Ras proteins can recruit effector proteins and turn on specific signaling pathways.
source: In the GTP-bound state, Ras proteins can recruit effector proteins and turn on specific signaling pathways (Hancock, 2003; Karnoub and Weinberg, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Protein post-translational modifications play important roles in regulating the Ras family of proteins.
source: Protein post-translational modifications (PTMs) play important roles in regulating the Ras family of proteins (Ahearn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ras and Rho families of GTPases are modified by prenylation on their C-terminal CaaX motif at the cysteine residue.
source: Ras and Rho families of GTPases are modified by prenylation (farnesylation or geranylgeranylation) on their C-terminal CaaX motif at the cysteine residue.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Ras protein modifications.

claim: H-Ras and N-Ras contain cysteine palmitoylation as a second lipidation.
source: Some proteins from Ras and Rho families, such as H-Ras and N-Ras, contain cysteine palmitoylation as a second lipidation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about specific Ras proteins.

claim: Prenylation and palmitoylation serve as important membrane targeting signals.
source: Both prenylation and palmitoylation serve as important membrane targeting signals (Ahearn et al., 2011; Linder and Deschenes, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: K-Ras4B does not have cysteine palmitoylation and is thought to use a C-terminal polybasic sequence for membrane targeting.
source: Other proteins from Ras and Rho families, such as K-Ras4B, do not have cysteine palmitoylation and are thought to use a C-terminal polybasic sequence for membrane targeting (Ahearn et al., 2011; Linder and Deschenes, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: R-Ras2 is also called TC21 because it was cloned from a human teratocarcinoma cDNA library.
source: Here, we demonstrate that a Ras family protein, R-Ras2 (also called TC21 because it was cloned from a human teratocarcinoma cDNA library) (Drivas et al., 1990), which is able to transform cells and is up-regulated in several human cancers (Lee et al., 2011; Gutierrez-Erlandsson et al., 2013; Erdogan et al., 2007; Murphy et al., 2002), is regulated by a novel PTM, lysine fatty acylation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: R-Ras2 is able to transform cells.
source: Here, we demonstrate that a Ras family protein, R-Ras2 (also called TC21 because it was cloned from a human teratocarcinoma cDNA library) (Drivas et al., 1990), which is able to transform cells and is up-regulated in several human cancers (Lee et al., 2011; Gutierrez-Erlandsson et al., 2013; Erdogan et al., 2007; Murphy et al., 2002), is regulated by a novel PTM, lysine fatty acylation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: R-Ras2 is up-regulated in several human cancers.
source: Here, we demonstrate that a Ras family protein, R-Ras2 (also called TC21 because it was cloned from a human teratocarcinoma cDNA library) (Drivas et al., 1990), which is able to transform cells and is up-regulated in several human cancers (Lee et al., 2011; Gutierrez-Erlandsson et al., 2013; Erdogan et al., 2007; Murphy et al., 2002), is regulated by a novel PTM, lysine fatty acylation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SIRT6 defatty-acylates R-Ras2 and attenuates its plasma membrane localization.
source: SIRT6 defatty-acylates R-Ras2 and attenuates its plasma membrane localization, therefore inhibits its ability to activate PI3K signaling pathway and cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: SIRT6 inhibits R-Ras2's ability to activate PI3K signaling pathway.
source: SIRT6 defatty-acylates R-Ras2 and attenuates its plasma membrane localization, therefore inhibits its ability to activate PI3K signaling pathway and cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: SIRT6 inhibits R-Ras2's ability to promote cell proliferation.
source: SIRT6 defatty-acylates R-Ras2 and attenuates its plasma membrane localization, therefore inhibits its ability to activate PI3K signaling pathway and cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction and supported by data in Figure 4D.

claim: SIRT6 has been reported to be a tumor suppressor.
source: SIRT6 has been reported to be a tumor suppressor (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Decreased SIRT6 expression level is found in several human cancers.
source: Decreased SIRT6 expression level is found in several human cancers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section.

claim: Enhanced glycolysis is observed in SIRT6-deficient cells and tumors.
source: Enhanced glycolysis is observed in SIRT6-deficient cells and tumors, which is thought to drive tumor formation in vivo (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Tumor formation promoted by the loss of SIRT6 is oncogene HRAS-independent.
source: Interestingly, the tumor formation promoted by the loss of SIRT6 is oncogene HRAS-independent.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section.

claim: SIRT6 G60A mutant maintains the defatty-acylase activity but exhibits no detectable deacetylase activity in cells.
source: We have recently identified a single point mutation (G60A) of SIRT6 that maintains the defatty-acylase activity but exhibits no detectable deacetylase activity in cells (Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Sirt6 KO MEFs expressing SIRT6 WT showed decreased cell proliferation compared to those without SIRT6 expression.
source: Sirt6 KO MEFs expressing SIRT6 WT showed decreased cell proliferation compared to those without SIRT6 expression (Figure 1A), consistent with the reported role of SIRT6 in suppressing cell proliferation.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cell proliferation assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression of SIRT6 H133Y mutant had no significant effect on cell proliferation in Sirt6 KO MEFs.
source: In contrast, expressing the H133Y mutant had no significant effect on cell proliferation.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cell proliferation assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression of SIRT6 G60A mutant decreased cell proliferation in Sirt6 KO MEFs, similar to the expression of SIRT6 WT.
source: Interestingly, expression of the G60A mutant, which only exhibits the defatty-acylase activity in cells, also decreased cell proliferation, similar to the expression of SIRT6 WT (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cell proliferation assay shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The defatty-acylase activity of SIRT6 plays a major role in regulating cell proliferation.
source: This suggests that although both deacetylase and defatty-acylase activities of SIRT6 contribute, the defatty-acylase activity plays a major role in regulating cell proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that G60A mutant (defatty-acylase only) has similar effect to WT in suppressing cell proliferation.

claim: 865 proteins were identified in Alk12 SILAC experiment.
source: There were 865 proteins identified in Alk12 SILAC and 1285 proteins identified in Alk14 SILAC (Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from the SILAC mass spectrometry experiment.

claim: 1285 proteins were identified in Alk14 SILAC experiment.
source: There were 865 proteins identified in Alk12 SILAC and 1285 proteins identified in Alk14 SILAC (Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a direct result from the SILAC mass spectrometry experiment.

claim: Five proteins were identified as potential SIRT6 defatty-acylation targets after filtering SILAC data.
source: With these criteria, we narrowed down the target lists to five proteins (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C after applying filtering criteria to SILAC data.

claim: R-Ras2 was one of the possible defatty-acylation targets of SIRT6 identified by SILAC.
source: Interestingly, a Ras-related small GTPase, R-Ras2, was one of the possible defatty-acylation targets of SIRT6.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C as one of the five proteins identified.

claim: Knockdown of R-Ras2 in both Sirt6 WT and KO MEFs significantly decreased cell proliferation.
source: Knockdown of R-Ras2 in both Sirt6 WT and KO MEFs by two different shRNAs significantly decreased cell proliferation (Figure 1D), suggesting that R-Ras2 is important for cell proliferation in MEFs.
evidence: This is directly observed in the cell proliferation assay shown in Figure 1D.

claim: R-Ras2 is important for cell proliferation in MEFs.
source: Knockdown of R-Ras2 in both Sirt6 WT and KO MEFs by two different shRNAs significantly decreased cell proliferation (Figure 1D), suggesting that R-Ras2 is important for cell proliferation in MEFs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that R-Ras2 knockdown decreases cell proliferation.

claim: SIRT6 did not affect the transcription and translation of R-Ras2.
source: The results showed that SIRT6 did not affect the transcription and translation of R-Ras2 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in Figure 2A showing similar mRNA and protein levels in Sirt6 WT and KO MEFs.

claim: R-Ras2 exhibited increased lysine fatty acylation in Sirt6 KO MEFs than in WT MEFs.
source: R-Ras2 exhibited increased lysine (NH2OH-resistant) fatty acylation in Sirt6 KO MEFs than in WT MEFs (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the in-gel fluorescence assay shown in Figure 2B.

claim: R-Ras2 lysine fatty acylation increased in HEK 293T cells after knocking down SIRT6.
source: We also observed increased R-Ras2 lysine fatty acylation in Human Embryonic Kidney (HEK) 293 T cells after knocking down SIRT6 with two different Sirt6 shRNAs, but not with a control shRNA (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the in-gel fluorescence assay shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Endogenous R-Ras2 contained more lysine fatty acylation in Sirt6 KO MEFs than in WT MEFs.
source: More fatty-acylated endogenous R-Ras2 was pulled down from Sirt6 KO MEFs than from WT MEFs (Figure 2D), suggesting that endogenous R-Ras2 contained more lysine fatty acylation in Sirt6 KO MEFs.
evidence: This is directly observed in the streptavidin pulldown assay shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SIRT6 removed most of the lysine fatty acylation signal from R-Ras2 in the presence of NAD+ in vitro.
source: In the presence of NAD+, SIRT6 removed most of the lysine fatty acylation signal from R-Ras2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is directly observed in the in vitro defatty-acylation assay shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SIRT6 WT, but not the catalytic mutant SIRT6 H133Y, generated the fatty acyl ADPR product in the presence of R-Ras2 and NAD+.
source: SIRT6 WT, but not the catalytic mutant SIRT6 H133Y, generated the fatty acyl ADPR spot in the presence of R-Ras2 isolated from Sirt6 KO MEFs and NAD+ (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is directly observed in the 32P-NAD+ assay shown in Figure 2F.

claim: R-Ras2 is fatty-acylated on lysine residues.
source: These data suggested that R-Ras2 was fatty-acylated on lysine residues and SIRT6 could directly remove the fatty acylation in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro defatty-acylation assays and 32P-NAD+ assay.

claim: SIRT6 could directly remove the fatty acylation from R-Ras2 in vitro.
source: These data suggested that R-Ras2 was fatty-acylated on lysine residues and SIRT6 could directly remove the fatty acylation in vitro.
evidence: This is inferred from the in vitro defatty-acylation assays and 32P-NAD+ assay.

claim: R-Ras2 contains four lysine residues in the C-terminal hypervariable region: K192, K194, K196, and K197.
source: We noticed that there are four lysine residues in the C-terminal hypervariable region (HVR) of R-Ras2: K192, K194, K196, and K197 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated based on the protein sequence shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The C-terminal hypervariable region of R-Ras2 is known as a C-terminal polybasic sequence.
source: This region is known as a C-terminal polybasic sequence and is generally believed to help anchor Ras proteins to the membrane through electrostatic interaction (Ahearn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The R-Ras2 4KR mutant significantly decreased the lysine fatty acylation signal in Sirt6 KO MEFs.
source: We examined the lysine fatty acylation of R-Ras2 WT and 4KR in Sirt6 KO MEFs and found that the 4KR mutant significantly decreased the lysine fatty acylation signal (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is directly observed in the in-gel fluorescence assay shown in Figure 2G.

claim: A peptide carrying Alk14 modification on K194 of R-Ras2 was detected by mass spectrometry.
source: A peptide (residue 193–197) carrying Alk14 modification on K194 was detected (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is directly observed in the MS/MS spectrum shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Single mutation of each of the four lysine residues (K192, K194, K196, K197) to arginine did not affect R-Ras2 lysine fatty acylation.
source: Interestingly, when we mutated each of these four lysine residues to arginine and detected their Alk14 labeling by in-gel fluorescence, the hydroxylamine-resistant labeling of all the single mutants was similar to that of WT (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is directly observed in the in-gel fluorescence assay shown in Figure 2I.

claim: K192, K194, K196, and K197 are likely to be fatty acylated redundantly on R-Ras2.
source: This result suggested that K192, K194, K196, and K197 are likely to be fatty acylated redundantly, although the MS result implied that K194 is preferentially fatty acylated on WT R-Ras2 protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that single mutations do not affect fatty acylation while the 4KR mutant does.

claim: K194 is preferentially fatty acylated on WT R-Ras2 protein.
source: This result suggested that K192, K194, K196, and K197 are likely to be fatty acylated redundantly, although the MS result implied that K194 is preferentially fatty acylated on WT R-Ras2 protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the MS data showing K194 modification.

claim: R-Ras2 has palmitoylation on cysteine 199.
source: R-Ras2 is known to have palmitoylation on cysteine 199, which is close to the fatty acylated lysine cluster.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Cysteine fatty acylation of R-Ras2 is not required for the occurrence of its lysine fatty acylation.
source: Alk14 labeling still occurred on R-Ras2 C199S mutant, which was NH2OH resistant (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that cysteine fatty acylation of R-Ras2 is not required for the occurrence of its lysine fatty acylation.
evidence: This is directly observed in the in-gel fluorescence assay shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: In Sirt6 WT MEFs, both R-Ras2 WT and 4KR were localized in the plasma membrane and intracellular vesicles.
source: In Sirt6 WT MEFs, both R-Ras2 WT and 4KR were localized in the plasma membrane and intracellular vesicles (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the confocal imaging shown in Figure 2J.

claim: In Sirt6 KO MEFs, R-Ras2 WT was mainly localized in the plasma membrane.
source: In contrast, in Sirt6 KO MEFs, R-Ras2 WT was mainly localized in the plasma membrane, while R-Ras2 4KR was localized in both the plasma membrane and intracellular vesicles (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the confocal imaging shown in Figure 2J.

claim: In Sirt6 KO MEFs, R-Ras2 4KR was localized in both the plasma membrane and intracellular vesicles.
source: In contrast, in Sirt6 KO MEFs, R-Ras2 WT was mainly localized in the plasma membrane, while R-Ras2 4KR was localized in both the plasma membrane and intracellular vesicles (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the confocal imaging shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation helps targeting R-Ras2 to the plasma membrane.
source: Considering that R-Ras2 WT in Sirt6 KO MEFs has the highest lysine fatty acylation level (Figure 2B and G), this data suggests that lysine fatty acylation helps targeting R-Ras2 to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the confocal imaging and fatty acylation data.

claim: Treatment with palmitic acid or SIRT6 inhibitor TM3 decreased cytosolic localization of WT R-Ras2, but not the 4KR mutant.
source: When we treated the cells with palmitic acid (to increase R-Ras2 lysine fatty acylation) or SIRT6 inhibitor TM3 (to inhibit SIRT6 defatty-acylase activity) (He et al., 2014), we observed decreased cytosolic localization of WT R-Ras2, but not the 4KR mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the subcellular fractionation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Expressing SIRT6 G60A mutant in Sirt6 KO MEFs decreased R-Ras2 lysine fatty acylation to the same level as expressing WT SIRT6.
source: Expressing the G60A mutant in Sirt6 KO MEFs decreased R-Ras2 lysine fatty acylation to the same level as expressing WT SIRT6 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the in-gel fluorescence assay shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SIRT6 G60A mutant removed fatty acylation from R-Ras2 similar to WT SIRT6 in vitro.
source: In vitro, the G60A mutant removed fatty acylation from R-Ras2 similar to WT SIRT6 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the in vitro defatty-acylation assay shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of SIRT6 G60A mutant in Sirt6 KO MEFs promoted R-Ras2 dissociation from the plasma membrane, similar to the expression of WT SIRT6.
source: Confocal imaging results showed that in Sirt6 KO MEFs, expression of the G60A mutant promoted R-Ras2 dissociation from the plasma membrane, similar to the expression of WT SIRT6 (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the confocal imaging shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SIRT6 G60A mutant decreased the plasma-membrane-localized endogenous R-Ras2 and increased the intracellular vesicle-localized endogenous R-Ras2, similar to WT SIRT6.
source: Subcellular fractionation of endogenous R-Ras2 showed that, similar to WT SIRT6, the G60A mutant decreased the plasma-membrane-localized endogenous R-Ras2 and increased the intracellular vesicle-localized endogenous R-Ras2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the subcellular fractionation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The defatty-acylase activity of SIRT6 is sufficient to regulate R-Ras2.
source: These data collectively demonstrated that the defatty-acylase activity of SIRT6 is sufficient to regulate R-Ras2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that G60A mutant (defatty-acylase only) regulates R-Ras2 similar to WT SIRT6.

claim: R-Ras2 has two well-studied effector pathways: the PI3K/Akt pathway and the Raf/MAPK pathway.
source: There are two well-studied effector pathways of R-Ras2, the PI3K/Akt pathway (Rong et al., 2002; Rosário et al., 2001) and the Raf/MAPK pathway (Rosário et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In MEFs, R-Ras2 was unlikely to activate the Raf/MAPK pathway.
source: The endogenous total Ras (H-Ras, N-Ras and K-Ras), but not the overexpressed or endogenous R-Ras2, was pulled down by Raf RBD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that in MEFs, R-Ras2 was unlikely to activate the Raf/MAPK pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the Raf RBD pulldown assay shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: WT R-Ras2 in Sirt6 KO MEFs had more p110α interaction than the WT R-Ras2 in Sirt6 WT MEFs or the 4KR mutant in either Sirt6 WT or KO MEFs.
source: WT R-Ras2 in Sirt6 KO MEFs, which was shown to have the highest level of lysine fatty acylation (Figure 2B and G), had more p110α interaction than the WT R-Ras2 in Sirt6 WT MEFs or the 4KR mutant in either Sirt6 WT or KO MEFs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the co-IP experiment shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation of R-Ras2 promotes its interaction with p110α.
source: This data suggested that lysine fatty acylation of R-Ras2 promotes its interaction with p110α.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-IP data showing increased interaction with higher fatty acylation.

claim: Sirt6 KO MEFs showed higher phosphorylated Akt on Thr308, but not on Ser473, when compared to Sirt6 WT MEFs.
source: Sirt6 KO MEFs showed higher phosphorylated Akt on Thr308 (p-Akt Thr308), but not on Ser473 (p-Akt Ser473), when compared to Sirt6 WT MEFs (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is directly observed in the Western blot shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Knockdown of R-Ras2 in Sirt6 WT MEFs did not affect p-Akt Thr308.
source: Knockdown of R-Ras2 in Sirt6 WT MEFs did not affect p-Akt Thr308, whereas knockdown of R-Ras2 in Sirt6 KO MEFs decreased p-Akt Thr308 to the same level as that in Sirt6 WT MEFs (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the Western blot shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Knockdown of R-Ras2 in Sirt6 KO MEFs decreased p-Akt Thr308 to the same level as that in Sirt6 WT MEFs.
source: Knockdown of R-Ras2 in Sirt6 WT MEFs did not affect p-Akt Thr308, whereas knockdown of R-Ras2 in Sirt6 KO MEFs decreased p-Akt Thr308 to the same level as that in Sirt6 WT MEFs (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the Western blot shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Expressing WT SIRT6 or the G60A mutant in Sirt6 KO MEFs decreased p-Akt Thr308 levels.
source: We further found that expressing WT SIRT6 or the G60A mutant in Sirt6 KO MEFs decreased p-Akt Thr308 levels (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that the defatty-acylation activity of SIRT6 is important for regulating p-Akt Thr308.
evidence: This is directly observed in the Western blot shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The defatty-acylation activity of SIRT6 is important for regulating p-Akt Thr308.
source: We further found that expressing WT SIRT6 or the G60A mutant in Sirt6 KO MEFs decreased p-Akt Thr308 levels (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that the defatty-acylation activity of SIRT6 is important for regulating p-Akt Thr308.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that G60A mutant (defatty-acylase only) decreases p-Akt Thr308.

claim: SIRT6 defatty-acylates R-Ras2 and attenuates its interaction with p110α, resulting in decreased Akt phosphorylation on Thr308.
source: All the data combined suggested that SIRT6 defatty-acylates R-Ras2 and attenuates its interaction with p110α, resulting in decreased Akt phosphorylation on Thr308.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on fatty acylation, p110α interaction, and Akt phosphorylation.

claim: Expression of R-Ras2 WT in Sirt6 KO MEFs significantly increased cell proliferation compared with vector control.
source: Expression of R-Ras2 WT in Sirt6 KO MEFs significantly increased cell proliferation compared with vector control (Figure 4D), while expressing R-Ras2 4KR in Sirt6 KO MEFs did not increase cell proliferation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cell proliferation assay shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Expressing R-Ras2 4KR in Sirt6 KO MEFs did not increase cell proliferation.
source: Expression of R-Ras2 WT in Sirt6 KO MEFs significantly increased cell proliferation compared with vector control (Figure 4D), while expressing R-Ras2 4KR in Sirt6 KO MEFs did not increase cell proliferation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cell proliferation assay shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In Sirt6 WT MEFs, neither overexpressing WT R-Ras2 nor the 4KR mutant increased cell proliferation compared with vector control.
source: In Sirt6 WT MEFs, neither overexpressing WT R-Ras2 nor the 4KR mutant increased cell proliferation compared with vector control (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the cell proliferation assay shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation of R-Ras2 is important for promoting MEF cell proliferation.
source: These data suggested that lysine fatty acylation of R-Ras2 is important for promoting MEF cell proliferation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only WT R-Ras2 (which can be fatty acylated), but not 4KR mutant, increases proliferation in Sirt6 KO MEFs.

claim: The defatty-acylase activity of SIRT6 is important for regulating cell proliferation.
source: In this study, we found that the defatty-acylase activity of SIRT6 is important for regulating cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 1A.

claim: R-Ras2 has a higher lysine fatty acylation level in Sirt6 KO MEFs than that in Sirt6 WT MEFs.
source: R-Ras2 has a higher lysine fatty acylation level in Sirt6 KO MEFs than that in Sirt6 WT MEFs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation targets R-Ras2 to the plasma membrane and facilitates its interaction with p110α.
source: Lysine fatty acylation targets R-Ras2 to the plasma membrane, facilitates its interaction with p110α, and activates the Akt signaling pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion and supported by data in Figures 2J and 4A.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation of R-Ras2 activates the Akt signaling pathway.
source: Lysine fatty acylation targets R-Ras2 to the plasma membrane, facilitates its interaction with p110α, and activates the Akt signaling pathway.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion and supported by data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: When R-Ras2 is knocked down or its lysine fatty acylation is decreased in Sirt6 KO MEFs, the p-Akt Thr308 level and cell proliferation become similar to those in Sirt6 WT MEFs.
source: This is important for the proliferative phenotype of Sirt6 KO MEFs because when we knocked down R-Ras2 or decreased its lysine fatty acylation in Sirt6 KO MEFs, the p-Akt Thr308 level and cell proliferation became similar to those in Sirt6 WT MEFs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion and supported by data in Figures 1D, 4B, and 4D.

claim: SIRT6 can function at the top of the signal transduction pathway by regulating a GTPase in the Ras family.
source: Now we showed that SIRT6 can also function at the top of the signal transduction pathway by regulating a GTPase in the Ras family.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion based on the findings of the study.

claim: SIRT6 is down-regulated in many different human cancers.
source: SIRT6 is known to be a tumor suppressor and down-regulated in many different human cancers (Sebastián et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Sirt6 KO increases lysine fatty acylation of R-Ras2 and activates the PI3K-Akt pathway, leading to higher cell proliferation.
source: Our study suggests that Sirt6 KO increases lysine fatty acylation of R-Ras2 and activates the PI3K-Akt pathway, leading to higher cell proliferation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion based on the findings of the study.

claim: The defatty-acylation and suppression of R-Ras2 is a major contributor to the tumor suppressor role of SIRT6.
source: Thus, the defatty-acylation and suppression of R-Ras2 is a major contributor to the tumor suppressor role of SIRT6.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion based on the findings of the study.

claim: K-Ras4B is thought to use polybasic sequences for membrane targeting.
source: For the Ras proteins that do not have palmitoylated cysteine (such as K-Ras4B), they are thought to use polybasic sequences for membrane targeting (Hancock, 2003; Cox et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: R-Ras2 contains several lysine residues at the C-terminus (Lys192, 194, 196, 197) in addition to palmitoylation on Cys199 and farnesylation on Cys201.
source: Interestingly, in addition to palmitoylation on Cys199 and farnesylation on Cys201, R-Ras2 contains several lysine residues at the C-terminus (Lys192, 194, 196, 197).
evidence: This is stated based on the protein sequence and known modifications.

claim: The lysine residues at the C-terminal of K-Ras4B play important roles for phospholipid binding and K-Ras4B signal output.
source: In a recent paper, the lysine residues at the C-terminal of K-Ras4B have been shown to play important roles for phospholipid binding and K-Ras4B signal output (Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The lysine to arginine mutant of K-Ras4B had distinct lipid-binding capacity.
source: The lysine to arginine mutant had distinct lipid-binding capacity, suggesting that simple electrostatic interaction may not be the mechanism how polybasic sequences target to the membrane.
evidence: This is stated based on previous literature findings.

claim: It is possible that the lysine residues at the C-terminal of K-Ras4B are similarly regulated by fatty acylation.
source: It is possible that the lysine residues at the C-terminal of K-Ras4B are similarly regulated by fatty acylation, which could explain the distinct lipid-binding capacity of the lysine-to-arginine mutant.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings for R-Ras2.

claim: Many Ras family of small GTPases contain polybasic sequences at the C-termini.
source: Many Ras family of small GTPases contain polybasic sequences at the C-termini.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about Ras family proteins.

claim: It is possible that lysine fatty acylation also occur on other Ras family GTPases and regulate their localization and activities.
source: It is possible that lysine fatty acylation also occur on these GTPases and regulate their localization and activities.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings for R-Ras2.

claim: Protein lysine fatty acylation was first reported in 1992.
source: Protein lysine fatty acylation was first reported in 1992 (Stevenson et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation regulates protein secretion (e.g. TNFα and ribosomal proteins).
source: We previously identified that lysine fatty acylation regulates protein secretion (e.g. TNFα and ribosomal proteins) (Jiang et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The finding that lysine fatty acylation regulates the Ras family of proteins suggests that this PTM may have very broad and important biological functions.
source: The finding that lysine fatty acylation regulates the Ras family of proteins suggest that this PTM may have very broad and important biological functions.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings of the study.

claim: p110α is one isoform of the catalytic subunit of PI3K.
source: We overexpressed FLAG-tagged R-Ras2 WT and 4KR in Sirt6 WT and KO MEFs, immunoprecipitated R-Ras2 and examined p110α, one isoform of the catalytic subunit of PI3K, which has been reported to interact with R-Ras2 (Rodriguez-Viciana et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: p110α has been reported to interact with R-Ras2.
source: We overexpressed FLAG-tagged R-Ras2 WT and 4KR in Sirt6 WT and KO MEFs, immunoprecipitated R-Ras2 and examined p110α, one isoform of the catalytic subunit of PI3K, which has been reported to interact with R-Ras2 (Rodriguez-Viciana et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: IpaJ is a cysteine protease from Shigella flexneri that hydrolyzes the peptide bond after N-myristoylated glycine.
source: When processing the samples, we used IpaJ, a cysteine protease from Shigella flexneri that has been reported to hydrolyze the peptide bond after N-myristoylated glycine (Burnaevskiy et al., 2013), to reduce the labeling background from N-myristoylation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.
